data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A single evaluation distinguishes genuine reliability gain by measuring whether the panel's errors, when they occur, are spread across orthogonal failure modes or concentrated in a single checklist-bypassable class; genuine reliability gain implies distributed independent errors (so averaging helps), while mere compliance implies correlated single-mode errors that averaging cannot fix and that happen to match the correct answer on the evaluated subset.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the checklist is so well-designed that it eliminates the independent errors but introduces no correlated error, the covariance will be low and the test will falsely signal a genuine averaging gain when it is actually checklist-driven.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the evaluation's sample size is too small for stable covariance estimation, the error-structure signal will be noise-dominated and uninformative within a single evaluation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Per SRC_005, the target confounds averaging independent errors with checklist compliance. If errors are independent, the panel's aggregate is more reliable than any single panelist. If errors are correlated because all panelists apply the same checklist surface, averaging does nothing, and the observed accuracy is entirely due to the checklist happening to track the answer. An error-structure analysis within one evaluation separates these: compute the covariance matrix of panelist errors; low off-diagonal covariance implies genuine averaging gain, high covariance implies mere compliance.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
